claims.source: To investigate this hypothesis and the role of actin in this process, we infected host cells with wt or act1 cKO parasites expressing GFP and bleached individual parasites within the PV before measuring the time of fluorescence recovery (Videos 1 and 2; Figure 2A). While the fluorescence signal recovered rapidly in wt parasites (~30 s), no fluorescence recovery could be observed in parasites depleted of actin, indicating a defect in material transfer (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Individual parasites remain connected via the intravacuolar network and can exchange cytoplasmic material.
claims.source: From this experiment, we concluded that individual parasites remain connected via the intravacuolar network and can exchange cytoplasmic material.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments.

claims.claim: The connections between parasites appear to be actin dependent.
claims.source: Furthermore, these connections appear to be actin dependent.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP experiments comparing wt and act1 cKO parasites.

claims.claim: Vesicles positive for GAPM1a-YFP were seen to be transported in wt parasites.
claims.source: To determine if vesicular as well as cytoplasmic material could be transferred between parasites, we performed time-lapse analysis of the integral membrane protein GAPM1a-YFP (Figure 2B) and identified vesicles moving in a directed manner, demonstrating that vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite (Figure 2B, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claims.claim: Vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite.
claims.source: To determine if vesicular as well as cytoplasmic material could be transferred between parasites, we performed time-lapse analysis of the integral membrane protein GAPM1a-YFP (Figure 2B) and identified vesicles moving in a directed manner, demonstrating that vesicular transport occurs outside of the parasite (Figure 2B, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 3.

claims.claim: Digital tracking of vesicles suggested a directional movement along a tubular or filamentous structure.
claims.source: Of note, digital tracking of vesicles suggested a directional movement along a tubular or filamentous structure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the digital tracking of vesicles.

claims.claim: Individual parasites within a vacuole remain connected via a network, possibly through the RB that is required to transfer both cytoplasmic and membrane bound material between individual parasites.
claims.source: In summary, these data indicate that individual parasites within a vacuole remain connected via a network, possibly through the RB that is required to transfer both cytoplasmic and membrane bound material between individual parasites.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Parasite actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of this interconnecting network.
claims.source: We hypothesize that parasite actin is required for the formation and/or maintenance of this interconnecting network.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: Upon transient expression of Cb fusion proteins, individual parasites within the PV remain connected by a filamentous actin network which stretches throughout the RB and parasitophorous vacuole.
claims.source: Upon transient expression of these proteins, we obtained identical staining of filamentous structures within the parasites. Cb was also localised somewhat diffusely in the parasite cytosol, probably corresponding to unbound Cb in the cytosol as the protein was expressed at a high level (Figure 3A). Strikingly, individual parasites within the PV remain connected by a filamentous actin network which stretches throughout the RB and parasitophorous vacuole and can be seen to enter the posterior pole of individual parasites (Figure 3A, arrow).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The majority of intracellular parasites appeared healthy with no apparent morphological changes during transient expressions of the Cb fusion proteins, indicating that expression of Cb-proteins is well tolerated by the parasite.
claims.source: During transient expressions of the fusion proteins, the majority of intracellular parasites appeared healthy with no apparent morphological changes, indicating that expression of Cb-proteins is well tolerated by the parasite.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the transient expression experiments.

claims.claim: Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility.
claims.source: Parasites stably expressing SAG1-ΔGPI-GFP (to label the dense granules) were transiently transfected with Cb-Halo and dense granule motility was analysed and correlated to mean fluorescent intensity of Cb-Halo within the parasite (Video 4; Figure 3C). Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility, however, weaker expression levels are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency (Figure 3C) or run length compared to controls (935 ± 39 nm vs 1013 ± 53 nm for control and Cb-Halo, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by dense granule motility data shown in Figure 3C and Video 4.

claims.claim: Weaker expression levels of Cb-Halo are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency or run length compared to controls.
claims.source: Parasites stably expressing SAG1-ΔGPI-GFP (to label the dense granules) were transiently transfected with Cb-Halo and dense granule motility was analysed and correlated to mean fluorescent intensity of Cb-Halo within the parasite (Video 4; Figure 3C). Strong expression of Cb-Halo leads to an almost complete block of dense granule motility, however, weaker expression levels are well tolerated with no significant change in either dense granule run frequency (Figure 3C) or run length compared to controls (935 ± 39 nm vs 1013 ± 53 nm for control and Cb-Halo, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by dense granule motility data shown in Figure 3C and Video 4.

claims.claim: Expression of Cb is well tolerated by the parasite indicating that it does not significantly adversely affect normal actin functions within the cell.
claims.source: In summary, expression of Cb is well tolerated by the parasite indicating that it does not significantly adversely affect normal actin functions within the cell, in agreement to data obtained in other cellular systems (Belin et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by citations to Belin et al., 2014; Panza et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Parasite growth, invasion, replication and egress rates are indistinguishable from wt parasites in stable parasite lines expressing either Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald.
claims.source: As transient transfection resulted in a heterologous population of parasites expressing Cb at varying levels, which may be deleterious for the parasites, we generated stable parasite lines expressing either Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald and confirmed that parasite growth, invasion, replication and egress rates are indistinguishable from wt parasites (Figure 4A–E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claims.claim: The rate of overall motility is slightly increased (p<0.05) upon expression of Cb.
claims.source: We found that the rate of overall motility is slightly increased (p<0.05) upon expression of Cb (Figure 4F), indicating an influence of Cb expression on actin dynamics.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites.
claims.source: Intriguingly, average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites (Figure 4G), while average gliding speed is reduced (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Average gliding speed is reduced in Cb expressing parasites.
claims.source: Intriguingly, average trajectory lengths are identical in wt and Cb expressing parasites (Figure 4G), while average gliding speed is reduced (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Parasites penetrate the host cell within 30 s irrespective of Cb expression.
claims.source: We also analysed average invasion speeds and confirmed that parasites penetrate the host cell within 30 s irrespective of Cb expression (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Time lapse imaging of Cb-Emerald demonstrated a highly dynamic behaviour of F-actin within the cytosol.
claims.source: Furthermore, time lapse imaging of Cb-Emerald demonstrated a highly dynamic behaviour of F-actin within the cytosol (Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 5.

claims.claim: The expression of this actin binding protein has no or modest effects on established actin-dependent processes in T. gondii.
claims.source: Together these data demonstrate that, similar to the situation in other eukaryotes, the expression of this actin binding protein has no or modest effects on established actin-dependent processes in T. gondii.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Recombinant Cb bound to chicken skeletal actin with Kd of 5 ± 1 µM.
claims.source: Recombinant Cb with a C-terminal 6-His tag (rCb) was expressed and purified from bacteria (Figure 5A,B). rCb bound to chicken skeletal actin with Kd of 5 ± 1 µM (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Only a small proportion of actin was precipitated in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, which corresponds well with published data suggesting that only ~2% of total parasite actin can be found in its filamentous form in extracellular parasites.
claims.source: To confirm that Cb-Halo binds specifically to Toxoplasma F-actin when expressed in the parasite, we co-immunoprecipitated actin from extracellular parasites using an anti-Halo antibody (Figure 5C). As expected, only a small proportion of actin was precipitated, which corresponds well with published data suggesting that only ~2% of total parasite actin can be found in its filamentous form in extracellular parasites (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997.

claims.claim: Mass-spectrometric analysis of the immunoprecipitation confirmed that Cb-Halo specifically precipitated parasite actin.
claims.source: Importantly, mass-spectrometric analysis of the immunoprecipitation confirmed that Cb-Halo specifically precipitated parasite actin.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: No host cell actin, actin related or actin-like proteins could be identified in the immunoprecipitation.
claims.source: Although additional, potential F-actin binding proteins were detected, no host cell actin, actin related or actin-like proteins could be identified (not shown).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: F-actin is barely detectable in extracellular parasites, indicating that it is primarily found in globular form.
claims.source: To assess if expression of Cb stabilises F-actin in parasites, we compared the amount of pelletable actin in parasites expressing Cb and wt parasites (Figure 5D). We confirmed that in both cases F-actin is barely detectable in extracellular parasites, indicating that it is primarily found in globular form.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Treatment of parasites with Jas allowed detection of significant amount of F-actin in the pellet.
claims.source: Treatment of parasites with Jas allowed detection of significant amount of F-actin in the pellet.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data.

claims.claim: No significant difference could be observed between control parasites and parasites expressing Cb in the amount of pelletable actin.
claims.source: Of note, no significant difference could be observed between control parasites and parasites expressing Cb.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sedimentation assay data.

claims.claim: Expression of Cb in parasites allows detection of F-actin and that Cb expression has only minor effects on F-actin dynamics.
claims.source: Together, these data confirm that expression of Cb in parasites allows detection of F-actin and that Cb expression has only minor effects on F-actin dynamics, as previously shown in other eukaryotes (Panza et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Panza et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Treatment of intracellular parasites with Cyt-D led to the disintegration of the inter-parasite connections with only punctate spots remaining.
claims.source: Using actin-modulating drugs, the actin cytoskeleton was either depolymerized with Cytochalasin D (Cyt-D) or stabilized with Jasplakinolide (Jas). Treatment of intracellular parasites with Cyt-D led to the disintegration of the inter-parasite connections with only punctate spots remaining, which were also identified with anti-actin antibody (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Treatment with Jas led to the stabilisation of F-actin and intra-parasite connections were easily detectable with either Cb or an anti-actin antibody.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment with Jas led to the stabilisation of F-actin and intra-parasite connections were easily detectable with either Cb or an anti-actin antibody (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In Jas-treated PVs, there is an increase in average and maximum filament size, together with a decrease in total number of short filaments.
claims.source: Using default settings of the Ridge Detector plugin (Steger, 1998) we determined the apparent number, maximum length and average filament size of PVs treated with Jas, Cyt-D or untreated PVs (control) (Figure 6A right panel). In Jas-treated PVs, and in contrast to Cyt-D treated PVs, there is an increase in average and maximum filament size, together with a decrease in total number of short filaments supporting the stabilisation and depolymerisation of Cb-Halo detected filaments in the presence of Jas and Cyt-D respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Cb-Halo is specifically labelling F-actin filaments and that Cb binding to actin does not prevent depolymerisation caused by Cyt-D.
claims.source: Overall, these results support that filaments detected with Cb-Halo behave as typical actin filaments in the presence of actin regulatory drugs. This supports the evidence that Cb-Halo is specifically labelling F-actin filaments and that Cb binding to actin does not prevent depolymerisation caused by Cyt-D.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with actin-modulating drugs.

claims.claim: As early as 24 hr after excision of the act1 gene, the filamentous network collapsed, leaving punctate actin spots visible only in the RBs.
claims.source: To confirm that parasite F-actin corresponds to Cb-positive structures, we expressed Cb-Halo in act1 cKO cells. Using these parasites, we found that as early as 24 hr after excision of the act1 gene, the filamentous network collapsed, leaving punctate actin spots visible only in the RBs (similar to vacuoles treated with Cyt-D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: By 48 hr onwards after excision of act1, no F-actin structures could be observed and Cb-Halo was completely cytosolic.
claims.source: By 48 hr onwards, no F-actin structures could be observed and Cb-Halo was completely cytosolic, as expected due to cytosolic expression of this reagent (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The loss of filaments within the act1 cKO over-time follows the down-regulation of ACT1 in act1 cKO, indicating a polymerisation mechanism similar to eukaryotic actins.
claims.source: The loss of filaments within the act1 cKO over-time follows the down-regulation of ACT1 in act1 cKO, indicating a polymerisation mechanism similar to eukaryotic actins (Whitelaw et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Latrunculin A treatment for 3 hr led to complete disruption of host cell F-actin, while the parasite F-actin network remained unaffected.
claims.source: To exclude a role of host cell actin in the formation of the inter-parasite connections, we treated infected host cells with the actin-disrupting drug latrunculin A, which specifically inhibits polymerization of host cell, but not parasite, actin (Hegge et al., 2010; Whitelaw et al., 2017). We found that latrunculin A treatment for 3 hr led to complete disruption of host cell F-actin (visualised using Phalloidin488), while the parasite F-actin network remained unaffected.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C and citations to Hegge et al., 2010; Whitelaw et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Cb-positive filamentous structures were not derived from host cell actin.
claims.source: This confirms that Cb-positive filamentous structures were not derived from host cell actin (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the latrunculin A treatment experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: In absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) - when ADF is expressed - parasite F-actin shows a highly dynamic behaviour similar to wt parasites.
claims.source: When we expressed Cb-Emerald in adf cKD to compare actin dynamics, we found that in absence of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) - when ADF is expressed - parasite F-actin shows a highly dynamic behaviour similar to wt parasites (Figure 6D, compare Videos 6 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Videos 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Incubation of parasites with ATc for 96 hr leads to depletion of ADF and consequently F-actin dynamics is significantly diminished.
claims.source: In stark contrast, incubation of parasites with ATc for 96 hr leads to depletion of ADF and consequently F-actin dynamics is significantly diminished.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data.

claims.claim: Upon depletion of ADF, F-actin filaments accumulate at the posterior and to a lesser extent at the apical pole of the parasites.
claims.source: Under these conditions F-actin filaments accumulate at the posterior and to a lesser extent at the apical pole of the parasites.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data.

claims.claim: Upon depletion of ADF, no dynamic behaviour can be detected and no filaments can be detected within the cytosol of the parasites.
claims.source: However, no dynamic behaviour can be detected and no filaments can be detected within the cytosol of the parasites (Figure 6D (red arrows), Videos 6 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6D and Videos 6 and 7.

claims.claim: In non-replicating parasites F-actin forms an extended, continuous filamentous network through the RB, connecting the parasites.
claims.source: Using time-lapse analysis, we found that in non-replicating parasites F-actin forms an extended, continuous filamentous network through the RB, connecting the parasites.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: During parasite replication, the F-actin network collapses and F-actin retreats to the RB before the network reform again, extending throughout the PV.
claims.source: During parasite replication, this network collapses and F-actin retreats to the RB (asterisks) before the network reform again, extending throughout the PV (Figure 7A, Video 8).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7A and Video 8.

claims.claim: The F-actin filaments appear relatively static in resting parasites and do not show much reorientation/movement within 8 hr.
claims.source: Note that these filaments appear relatively static in resting parasites and do not show much reorientation/movement within 8 hr.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: Once parasites start to replicate within the PV, the connections disintegrate and F-actin appears to be restricted to the RB.
claims.source: However, once parasites start to replicate within the PV, the connections disintegrate and F-actin appears to be restricted to the RB (Figures 7A and 8A, Videos 8 and 12).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figures 7A and 8A, Videos 8 and 12.

claims.claim: The F-actin network collapses rapidly, between 10 and 60 s after Ca2+-Ionophore addition.
claims.source: When we triggered a calcium signalling cascade using Ca2+-Ionophore (Black et al., 2000), the F-actin network collapsed rapidly, between 10 and 60 s after Ca2+-Ionophore addition (Figure 7B, Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Video 9, and a citation to Black et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Collapse of the network preceded the initiation of motility and egress from the host cell.
claims.source: Collapse of the network preceded the initiation of motility and egress from the host cell (Figure 7B, arrow head; Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7B and Video 9.

claims.claim: As the parasites begin to move away from the lysed host cell, F-actin can be detected at the rear of the parasites.
claims.source: As the parasites begin to move away from the lysed host cell, F-actin can be detected at the rear of the parasites (Figure 7B, inset) and residual filamentous actin is still seen within the RB.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Extracellular F-actin filaments reside within membranous tubules of 50–60 nm in diameter.
claims.source: To investigate the presence of F-actin within this network, we performed correlative light-electron microscopy (CLEM). The network within a vacuole was imaged using 3D structural illumination super-resolution microscopy (3D-SIM) (Figure 7C). Thin sections of the same network were then imaged with transmission electron microscopy (squares). This demonstrated that extracellular F-actin filaments reside within membranous tubules of 50–60 nm in diameter.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Within these tubules, several ~5 nm thick filaments extending over 100 nm in length were observed.
claims.source: Within these tubules, several ~5 nm thick filaments (arrows) extending over 100 nm in length were observed (highlighted in magenta).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by CLEM data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The membranous network consists of bundles of actin filaments bound within a membranous network, which connects individual parasites within the PV.
claims.source: Taken together these results confirm the presence of bundles of actin filaments bound within a membranous network, which connects individual parasites within the PV.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CLEM data.

claims.claim: F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s.
claims.source: Given that the inter-parasite tubules are reorganized during both replication and egress, we investigated the dynamic behaviour of F-actin within individual tubules using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). While F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast (Video 10) and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s (Figure 7D), we found that F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover (Video 11).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7D and Video 10.

claims.claim: F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover.
claims.source: Given that the inter-parasite tubules are reorganized during both replication and egress, we investigated the dynamic behaviour of F-actin within individual tubules using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). While F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol is very fast (Video 10) and recovery rates very rapid, within 20 s (Figure 7D), we found that F-actin within the tubular network is much more stable and fluorescence labelling of these structures took more than 60 s to fully recover (Video 11).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7D and Video 11.

claims.claim: There is the presence of highly dynamic, intracellular F-actin and a stable F-actin containing filamentous network.
claims.source: This demonstrates the presence of highly dynamic, intracellular F-actin and a stable F-actin containing filamentous network (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRAP data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: During early stages of daughter cell formation, F-actin was found in the RB linking the two parasites at their posterior end.
claims.source: Finally, given that act1 cKO parasites divided asynchronously we wanted to readdress the role of actin in parasite replication. We generated parasites co-expressing GAPM1a-YFP and Cb-Halo and performed live imaging (Figure 8A, Video 12). During early stages of daughter cell formation, F-actin was found in the RB linking the two parasites at their posterior end (Figure 8A; 1.24–2.36 hr).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A and Video 12.

claims.claim: At the earliest stages of daughter cell construction, F-actin accumulated at the elongating IMC.
claims.source: At the earliest stages of daughter cell construction, F-actin accumulated at the elongating IMC (Figure 8A: 1.36–2.36 hr) and further concentrated towards the posterior end of the mother cells, where it colocalized with the mother IMC (Figure 8A, 3.00–3.24 hr).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: As the daughters begin to bud from the maternal cell, the IMC of the mother disintegrates and appears to be transported towards the daughter cells.
claims.source: As the daughters begin to bud from the maternal cell, the IMC of the mother disintegrates and appears to be transported towards the daughter cells (Figure 8A, Arrows, 3.24–3.48 hr).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: At the end of replication, the now mature parasites remain connected through F-actin structures.
claims.source: At the end of replication, the now mature parasites remain connected through F-actin structures (Figure 8A, 4.00–5.12 hr).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: GAPM1a-YFP vesicles moved outside the parasite along filamentous tubules.
claims.source: Given that GAPM1a-YFP positive vesicles appear to be transported between individual parasites within a PV or between parasites and the residual body (Figures 2B and 8A) we wished to further define the role the filamentous network plays in this process. We imaged Cb-Halo and GAPM1a-YFP co-expressing parasites and tracked the motion of vesicles within the residual body. GAPM1a-YFP vesicles moved outside the parasite along filamentous tubules (Figure 8B), demonstrating vesicular transport within the residual body, as also shown for wt parasites (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Transport of vesicles was dependent on F-actin, as incubation of parasites with Cyt-D significantly abrogated vesicular transport.
claims.source: Importantly, transport of vesicles was dependent on F-actin, as incubation of parasites with Cyt-D significantly abrogated vesicular transport (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Individual parasites remain connected via an F-actin containing network that is required to transfer material in an active, F-actin dependent process.
claims.source: In summary, these data demonstrate that individual parasites remain connected via an F-actin containing network that is required to transfer material in an active, F-actin dependent process (Video 13).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Studies on Toxoplasma actin performed in the 90's suggested that apicomplexan actin is highly divergent and incapable of forming stable filaments.
claims.source: Studies on Toxoplasma actin performed in the 90's suggested that apicomplexan actin is highly divergent and incapable of forming stable filaments (Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997; Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1997; Dobrowolski et al., 1997; Dobrowolski and Sibley, 1996.

claims.source: Since then, polymerization kinetics of heterologously expressed apicomplexan actin showed that it polymerized in an unusual isodesmic process, in contrast to conventional eukaryotic actin (Skillman et al., 2013).

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2015.

claims.source: Parasite actin does not bind phalloidin, the gold standard reagent in other eukaryotic systems (Skillman et al., 2011) and, attempts to use genetically encoded actin sensors, such a LifeAct (Riedl et al., 2008) or Utrophin-CH (Burkel et al., 2007) have failed thus far (our and others unpublished data).

results.result: Actin depletion in T. gondii parasites results in loss of the residual body, asynchronous replication, disorganized growth within the parasitophorous vacuole, and aberrant posterior pole morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C40 collectively demonstrate that act1 cKO parasites lack a residual body (C27), grow asynchronously (C28, C36), lack inter-parasite connections (C37-C38), and show aberrant morphology (C39). These observations are supported by multiple imaging modalities including immunofluorescence and SEM (Figures 1A-C), providing converging evidence for actin's role in residual body formation and parasite organization.

results.result: Actin is required for material transfer between parasites within the parasitophorous vacuole, including both cytoplasmic and vesicular transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 demonstrate through FRAP experiments that wild-type parasites show rapid fluorescence recovery (~30s) while act1 cKO parasites show no recovery (C43-C44), indicating actin-dependent material transfer. Time-lapse imaging of GAPM1a-YFP vesicles (C47-C48) provides additional evidence for vesicular transport. The data from Figure 2A and Videos 1-3 provide strong experimental support.

results.result: Using chromobody (Cb) as a novel F-actin probe, an extensive filamentous actin network was visualized connecting parasites within the parasitophorous vacuole for the first time in live T. gondii.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C33, C115-C117 describe the successful visualization of F-actin networks using chromobody technology. The imaging data in Figure 3A-B clearly shows filamentous networks connecting parasites through the residual body and extending throughout the PV. This represents a major technical advance and novel biological finding, as conventional F-actin probes failed in this system (C29-C30).

results.result: Stable expression of chromobody (Cb-Halo or Cb-Emerald) is well tolerated by parasites with no or modest effects on actin-dependent processes including invasion, replication, egress, and motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C64 demonstrate through multiple functional assays (Figure 4A-H) that stable Cb expression does not significantly impair parasite growth, invasion, replication, or egress (C58). While high transient expression inhibits dense granule motility (C55), stable expression shows only modest effects on motility parameters (C59-C61). The comprehensive phenotypic characterization supports Cb as a valid tool for F-actin visualization.

results.result: Chromobody specifically binds to parasite F-actin without altering the total amount of F-actin in the parasite.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C72 provide biochemical validation of Cb specificity. The Kd measurement with chicken actin (C65), co-immunoprecipitation showing specific actin binding (C66-C67), exclusion of host actin (C68), and sedimentation assays showing no change in F-actin levels upon Cb expression (C69-C71) collectively demonstrate that Cb is a specific F-actin probe that does not artificially stabilize actin. Data in Figure 5 support these conclusions.

results.result: Cb-positive structures correspond to parasite F-actin, as demonstrated by sensitivity to actin-modulating drugs, dependence on act1 gene, and insensitivity to latrunculin A treatment that disrupts host but not parasite actin.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C81 provide multiple lines of evidence that Cb specifically labels parasite F-actin. Treatment with Cyt-D causes network disintegration while Jas stabilizes it (C73-C75), with quantitative filament analysis supporting these observations (C75). The network collapses upon act1 deletion (C77-C78), and latrunculin A treatment disrupts host but not parasite F-actin (C80-C81). Figure 6A-C provides strong supporting data.

results.result: Depletion of actin depolymerization factor (ADF) abolishes F-actin dynamics within the parasite cytosol and causes F-actin accumulation at the posterior and apical poles.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 and C143 demonstrate that ADF depletion dramatically affects F-actin dynamics. In the presence of ADF, F-actin shows highly dynamic behavior (C82), but upon ADF depletion, dynamics are abolished (C83, C85) and F-actin accumulates at parasite poles (C84). Figure 6D and Videos 6-7 provide clear visual evidence supporting these claims.

results.result: The F-actin network is highly dynamic throughout the parasite cell cycle, collapsing during replication and egress, and reforming during interphase.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 describe the dynamic reorganization of the F-actin network during the parasite lifecycle. Time-lapse imaging (Figure 7A, Video 8) shows the network extends through the PV in non-replicating parasites (C86), collapses during replication (C87, C89), and rapidly collapses (10-60s) upon calcium ionophore treatment before egress (C90-C91). The temporal resolution and visual documentation provide strong support.

results.result: Correlative light-electron microscopy reveals that F-actin filaments (~5 nm thick, >100 nm long) reside within membranous tubules of 50-60 nm diameter connecting parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 provide ultrastructural characterization of the F-actin network using CLEM. The combination of 3D-SIM and TEM (Figure 7C) directly demonstrates that F-actin filaments of appropriate dimensions (C94) are contained within membranous tubules (C93), confirming the network structure at high resolution. This provides definitive structural evidence for the F-actin-containing network.

results.result: F-actin exhibits distinct dynamics in different cellular compartments: highly dynamic with rapid recovery (~20s) in the parasite cytosol versus stable with slow recovery (>60s) in the inter-parasite tubular network.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 demonstrate differential F-actin dynamics using FRAP. The data in Figure 7D and Videos 10-11 clearly show rapid recovery in the cytosol (C96) versus slow recovery in tubules (C97), indicating distinct F-actin populations with different stability (C98). This finding reveals functional compartmentalization of the actin cytoskeleton.

results.result: During parasite replication, F-actin localizes to the residual body, accumulates at the elongating daughter IMC, concentrates at the posterior end during budding, and is involved in recycling the maternal IMC.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 and C34 describe F-actin localization during replication using live imaging of parasites co-expressing GAPM1a-YFP and Cb-Halo (Figure 8A, Video 12). The temporal sequence shows F-actin at the RB (C99), at the elongating IMC (C100), during IMC disintegration and transport (C101), and maintaining connections post-replication (C102). The high-resolution time-lapse data provide strong support.

results.result: Vesicular transport along F-actin filaments occurs within the residual body and is dependent on F-actin, as demonstrated by Cyt-D treatment abolishing vesicle movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 demonstrate F-actin-dependent vesicular transport. Imaging shows GAPM1a-YFP vesicles moving along Cb-Halo-labeled filaments (C103, Figure 8B), and Cyt-D treatment significantly reduces vesicle transport (C104, Figure 8C). The combination of visualization and pharmacological inhibition provides strong evidence for F-actin-dependent transport.

results.result: F-actin is required for residual body formation and/or maintenance, and the residual body network enables both cytoplasmic diffusion and vesicular transport between parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 synthesize the major findings regarding F-actin's role in residual body function. The combination of reverse genetics (act1 cKO lacking residual body, C133) and functional assays (FRAP showing material transfer, C134) provides strong evidence. This represents a major conclusion integrating multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: F-actin organization is highly dynamic throughout the parasite cell cycle, with distinct patterns during interphase, replication, budding, and egress.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C141 provide a comprehensive description of F-actin dynamics throughout the lifecycle. The data in Figures 8-9 show extended networks in interphase (C136), collapse during replication (C137), concentration at daughter IMC (C138), reformation during budding (C139), collapse during egress (C140), and concentration at the basal end during motility (C141). This represents a major integrative finding.

results.result: T. gondii infection causes no major complications in healthy individuals but can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals and fetuses infected in utero.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 present established clinical knowledge about T. gondii pathogenesis. These are well-documented facts in the field and provide appropriate context for the study, though they are not novel findings of this work.

results.result: T. gondii replicates via endodyogeny, with remnants of the mother cell forming the residual body that organizes parasites into a rosette pattern and maintains membrane connections until egress.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 describe established knowledge about T. gondii replication and residual body structure, supported by citations to Francia and Striepen 2014, and Muñiz-Hernández et al. 2011. These provide important background context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Previous studies showed that microtubule inhibitors cause structural collapse while actin-modulating drugs cause only slight replication defects, and parasite actin has crucial roles in invasion and egress.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 summarize prior work on cytoskeletal roles in T. gondii, citing Shaw et al. 2000 and Dobrowolski and Sibley 1996. These establish the historical context that motivated the current study but are not new findings.

results.result: Recent studies have implicated actin and myosins in intracellular processes including apicoplast division, dense granule transport, and parasite replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 cite recent literature (Egarter et al. 2014, Heaslip et al. 2016, Haase et al. 2015) establishing emerging roles for actin beyond invasion/egress. This provides important context for the current work but represents prior findings.

results.result: T. gondii actin is encoded by a single essential gene (act1) with ~80% identity to mammalian actins, is believed to be intrinsically unstable forming only short filaments, and exists 97% in globular form.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 summarize established biochemical properties of T. gondii actin from prior literature (Dobrowolski et al. 1997, Skillman et al. 2011). These provide essential background but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Apicomplexan actin has been proposed to polymerize via an unusual isodesmic mechanism, though this has been questioned due to misfolding of heterologously expressed actin, and in vivo F-actin formation depends on critical monomer concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 summarize the controversy regarding apicomplexan actin polymerization mechanisms, citing Skillman et al. 2013, Olshina et al. 2016, and Whitelaw et al. 2017. This establishes the scientific controversy motivating the current study but represents prior work.

results.result: Imaging studies in Plasmodium falciparum demonstrated extensive F-actin cytoskeleton in gametocytes and ookinetes, organized below the IMC rather than between IMC and plasma membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 cite work in related parasites (Hliscs et al. 2015, Siden-Kiamos et al. 2012) showing F-actin networks in other apicomplexans. This provides comparative context but is not a finding of the current study.

results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 establish the technical challenge (failure of conventional probes) and rationale for using chromobody technology. While C29-C30 represent knowledge from failed attempts, C31-C32 cite successful chromobody applications in other systems (Rocchetti et al. 2014, Panza et al. 2015), providing justification for the approach.

results.result: Initially, intracellular act1 cKO parasites replicate at comparable rates to wild-type parasites.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 cites Egarter et al. 2014 showing initial normal replication rates in act1 cKO. This provides context for understanding the later asynchronous phenotype but is a prior finding.

results.result: Historical studies suggested apicomplexan actin is highly divergent and incapable of forming stable filaments, with unusual isodesmic polymerization, but these findings have been questioned due to misfolding of heterologously expressed actin.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 summarize the historical controversy in the Discussion section, citing Dobrowolski and Sibley 1997, Skillman et al. 2013, and Olshina et al. 2016. This provides context for interpreting the current findings but represents prior work.

results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 cite recent literature establishing diverse actin functions (Andenmatten et al. 2013, Egarter et al. 2014, Haase et al. 2015, Heaslip et al. 2016, Foth et al. 2006). This provides context in the Discussion but represents prior findings.

results.result: Parasite actin does not bind phalloidin, and attempts to use genetically encoded sensors (LifeAct, Utrophin-CH) have failed.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 reiterate the technical challenges with conventional F-actin probes in the Discussion, citing Skillman et al. 2011, Riedl et al. 2008, and Burkel et al. 2007, plus unpublished data. This reinforces the significance of the chromobody approach.

results.result: Chromobodies have been successfully used in diverse eukaryotes to analyze actin dynamics and appear to have less toxicity than other F-actin sensors.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 cites prior chromobody applications (Panza et al. 2015, Plessner et al. 2015, Rocchetti et al. 2014) in the Discussion. This provides context for the validation experiments but represents prior work.

results.result: High transient Cb expression inhibits dense granule motility, but stable expression shows no effect on invasion, replication, and egress, with only small alterations in dense granule movement and motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 summarize the validation results in the Discussion, referencing Figure 4 data. This represents a synthesis of findings already presented in the Results section.

results.result: The total amount of F-actin does not change upon Cb expression, though actin dynamics may be modulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 summarize the sedimentation assay results (Figure 5) in the Discussion. This represents a synthesis of findings already presented in the Results section.

results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 summarize the drug sensitivity and act1 cKO validation experiments (Figure 6) in the Discussion. This represents a synthesis and conclusion from findings already presented in the Results section.

results.result: Actin presence in the RB and inter-parasite tubules was independently verified using α-actin antibody, which shows more prominent staining after Jas stabilization, though F-actin may be less accessible to antibodies after fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 describe independent validation of F-actin localization using antibodies (Figure 6) in the Discussion. C130 is speculative regarding antibody accessibility. This represents additional validation of the main findings.

results.result: The F-actin-containing membranous network in T. gondii appears similar to structures in Theileria annulata that contain F-actin in a similar configuration.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 draws a comparison to related parasites (Kühni-Boghenbor et al. 2012) in the Discussion. This provides comparative context but does not represent a novel finding of the current study.

results.result: The network may consist of short F-actin bundles cross-linked by unknown proteins, or actin binding proteins may coordinate to produce longer filaments in vivo than in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claim C142 is explicitly speculative ('we speculate') regarding the molecular organization of the F-actin network. While the speculation is reasonable and cites relevant literature (Skillman et al. 2011, Olshina et al. 2016, Salamun et al. 2014), it represents a hypothesis requiring further investigation rather than a demonstrated finding.

results.result: Defining cytosolic filament organization will be critical for understanding F-actin roles in vesicle transport and motility/invasion, where parasites devoid of actin remain invasive, possibly due to parasite modulation of host cell actin-driven membrane dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 discuss future directions and cite recent work (Whitelaw et al. 2017, Bichet et al. 2016) showing actin-independent invasion. This represents discussion of implications and future work rather than findings of the current study.

results.result: F-actin may be organized into distinct higher-order structures, forming large stable bundles in tubules while existing as single filaments or small bundles in the cytosol.
results.evaluation: Claim C147 is explicitly speculative ('it is possible') regarding F-actin organization into distinct structures. While consistent with the FRAP data showing differential dynamics, this represents a hypothesis requiring further structural characterization.
